archetypes.name: Rectangular microstrip patch
archetypes.summary: The standard half-wave rectangular patch on a grounded dielectric substrate.

synthesis.notes: Balanis 14-6: the width that gives good radiation efficiency without higher modes
Balanis 14-2: the electrical length each radiating edge gains from fringing

analysis.notes: surface-wave loss becomes significant above about 0.02 on high-permittivity substrates
Balanis: a single patch runs 5-7 (7-8 dBi); 6.6 is the standard thin-substrate figure
Standard closed form for a thin substrate; accurate to roughly 20% for h/lambda0 < 0.02. Bandwidth is set by h and eps_r, not by patch area.

validity: W/h > 1 for the eps_reff expression
h < 0.05*lambda0; thicker substrates need a probe-inductance correction
transmission-line model ignores surface waves and mutual edge coupling; expect 1-3% error in f0 and more on high-permittivity substrates
single-layer, isotropic, non-magnetic substrate

known_cases.source: Balanis Example 14.1: f0 = 10 GHz, eps_r = 2.2, h = 0.1588 cm gives W = 1.186 cm, L = 0.906 cm
Standard FR-4 2.4 GHz patch: W = 38.0 mm, L = 29.2 mm. Garg, Bhartia, Bahl & Ittipiboon, Microstrip Antenna Design Handbook

references: Garg, Bhartia, Bahl & Ittipiboon, Microstrip Antenna Design Handbook

archetypes.name: Inset-fed rectangular patch
archetypes.summary: Rectangular patch with a microstrip inset feed cut to reach a target input resistance.

synthesis.notes: Balanis 14-12, the W/lambda0 < 1 branch of the slot conductance

Balanis 14-17 including the mutual conductance between the two radiating slots, with G12 approximated as G1*J0(k0*L). Neglecting G12 entirely overestimates Rin by 26% (288 vs 228 ohm on the Example 14.1 patch), so it cannot be ignored. DISCREPANCY WORTH KNOWING: this J0 form lands within 1.7% of the 228.35 ohm Balanis quotes in Example 14.2, but numerically integrating eq. 14-18a directly gives 212.5 ohm (6.9% below the quoted value). The two disagree; treat any inset depth from this model as a starting point to verify in a full-wave solver.
Inverts Rin(y0) = Rin0*cos^2(pi*y0/L) (Balanis 14-20). The cos^2 law degrades for deep insets and wide notches; verify in a solver.

analysis.notes: should return Z_target by construction

validity: cos^2 inset law is an approximation; error grows past y0/L ~ 0.35
mutual conductance between the two radiating slots is neglected in Rin0
W/h > 1, h < 0.05*lambda0
mutual slot conductance is approximated as G1*J0(k0*L); the exact integral of eq. 14-18a disagrees with the published example by 6.9%, so inset depths carry real uncertainty

known_cases.source: Self-consistency: the synthesised inset depth must reproduce the target resistance through the independent forward cos^2 relation. Balanis 4th ed. eq. 14-20.
Balanis Example 14.2: Rin = 228.35 ohm at the radiating edge of the Example 14.1 patch, with mutual slot conductance included. The G1*J0(k0*L) model reproduces this to 1.7%.
Targeting a resistance at the edge value must place the inset at the edge (y0/L -> 0), confirming the cos^2 inversion is self-consistent.

references: Garg, Bhartia, Bahl & Ittipiboon, Microstrip Antenna Design Handbook

archetypes.name: Circular microstrip patch
archetypes.summary: Circular patch resonating in the dominant TM11 mode.

synthesis.notes: Balanis 14-65; the 8.791e9 constant carries the unit conversion, so F is dimensionless only in the cgs-derived form the reference uses
Balanis 14-64. Written in cm internally (hence the 100 factors) to match the reference constants, then converted back to metres.

analysis.notes: Balanis 14-66, the fringing-corrected radius
Forward check: TM11 resonance from the effective radius. 1.8412 is the first zero of J1'. Must return f0.
marginally below a rectangular patch of the same resonance

validity: h << lambda0 and h/a small; the fringing model degrades for thick substrates
TM11 only; TM21 appears at about 1.66*f0
cgs-derived constants: the synthesis expression converts explicitly

known_cases.source: Balanis Example 14.4: f0 = 10 GHz, eps_r = 2.2, h = 0.1588 cm gives a = 0.525 cm

archetypes.name: Planar inverted-F antenna (PIFA)
archetypes.summary: Shorted quarter-wave patch; the standard internal antenna in handsets.

synthesis.notes: Full-width short (Ws = W): L + h = lambda/4. The general case interpolates toward L + W + h = lambda/4 as Ws/W falls, per Hirasawa & Haneishi.

analysis.notes: limiting case as the shorting strip narrows to a pin
Indicative: PIFA bandwidth scales with height above ground. Roughly 30% accurate; real handset PIFAs are dominated by the ground-plane resonance.
Indicative. A PIFA's pattern is largely set by the ground plane it sits on, not by the plate; treat this as a placeholder until simulated.

validity: h << lambda0
assumes a ground plane large compared with the plate; handset ground planes are not, and the ground plane usually radiates more than the PIFA does
bandwidth and directivity entries are indicative, not derived

known_cases.source: lambda/4 at 1.8 GHz = 41.64 mm; full-width short gives L = 41.64 - 6 = 35.64 mm. Hirasawa & Haneishi, Analysis, Design and Measurement of Small and Low-Profile Antennas

references: Hirasawa & Haneishi, Analysis, Design and Measurement of Small and Low-Profile Antennas
Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 14 Ch. 14

archetypes.name: Quarter-wave shorted patch
archetypes.summary: Rectangular patch cut in half at its voltage null and shorted there: half the length, one radiating edge.

synthesis.notes: unchanged from the full patch - only the length is halved

A QUARTER wavelength, with only ONE fringing extension subtracted - the shorted edge has no fringing field. Since the full patch subtracts two, the shorted length works out to exactly half the full one.
what a conventional patch would need, for comparison

analysis.notes: Exactly 0.5 in this model: the fringing extension scales with the number of open edges, so it halves along with the length rather than leaving a residue. Real shorted patches come out a little longer than half, because a finite shorting wall is not a perfect electric wall.

Exactly 0.5 in this model: the fringing extension scales with the number of open edges, so it halves along with the length rather than leaving a residue. Real shorted patches come out a little longer than half, because a finite shorting wall is not a perfect electric wall.
Indicative. One radiating slot instead of two costs about 3 dB against the full patch's 6.6, and the pattern tilts toward the open edge. Treat as a placeholder, not a computed value.
Roughly half the full patch's: the stored energy is nearly unchanged while only one slot radiates, so Q about doubles. Indicative.
A FULL-width short holds the field distribution closest to the half-patch ideal. Narrowing it toward a single pin turns this into a PIFA, which resonates lower again for the same length.

validity: h << lambda0, as for any cavity-model patch
assumes an ideal full-width shorting wall; real shorting posts or a partial wall shift the resonance downward
directivity and bandwidth figures are indicative, scaled from the full patch rather than computed
the pattern is asymmetric - the single radiating edge tilts the beam off broadside, which the full patch's symmetry avoids

known_cases.source: Exactly one half, algebraically: L = lambda_g/4 - dL against L_full = lambda_g/2 - 2*dL. The shorted patch is precisely half the full patch in this model, not merely close to it.

2.4 GHz on 1.6 mm FR-4: W = (c/2f)*sqrt(2/5.4) = 38.01 mm, unchanged from a full patch. eps_reff = 4.0858, dL = 0.739 mm, so L = c/(4f*sqrt(eps_reff)) - dL = 14.71 mm. Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 14.2 for the underlying cavity model.

references: Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 14.2 (transmission-line model)
Garg, Bhartia, Bahl & Ittipiboon, Microstrip Antenna Design Handbook, Artech 2001, Ch. 9

archetypes.name: Equilateral triangular patch
archetypes.summary: Equilateral triangle in a cavity: about 40 percent less copper than a rectangular patch at the same frequency.

synthesis.notes: Inverted from f_mn = (2c/(3*a_eff*sqrt(eps_r)))*sqrt(m^2+mn+n^2) for the dominant TM10, with the usual a_eff = a + h/sqrt(eps_r) fringing correction backed out.

analysis.notes: forward check: must return f0
Exactly 2/3 for the dominant mode, independent of substrate - the triangle's defining proportion
an equivalent rectangular patch, ignoring its fringing correction, for comparison
About 0.60-0.66 depending on permittivity: the compactness that makes the triangle worth the awkward feed geometry
sqrt(m^2+mn+n^2) = sqrt(3) for TM11 - the first higher mode, 1.732*f0
TM20 at exactly twice the fundamental
Indicative. A triangular patch runs roughly 1 dB below a rectangular one because its aperture is smaller. Placeholder, not computed.
the rectangular-patch estimate with W/L set to 1; indicative for this shape

validity: h << lambda0; the cavity model assumes a single z-directed field with magnetic side walls
the a_eff = a + h/sqrt(eps_r) correction is the common first-order one and loses accuracy on thick or low-permittivity substrates
feed placement along a median sets the impedance and is not solved here
directivity is indicative

known_cases.source: f = 2c/(3*a*sqrt(eps_r)) gives a_eff = 134.75 mm at 1 GHz on eps_r = 2.2, less the 1.08 mm fringing correction. The side is exactly two thirds of a guided wavelength for the dominant mode, whatever the substrate.
77.4 cm^2 against the rectangular patch's 119.8 cm^2 at the same frequency - the triangle needs about 36% less board area
Mode spectrum follows sqrt(m^2+mn+n^2): 1, sqrt(3), 2. Garg et al., Microstrip Antenna Design Handbook, Ch. 7

references: Garg, Bhartia, Bahl & Ittipiboon, Microstrip Antenna Design Handbook, Artech 2001, Ch. 7
Helszajn & James, Planar triangular resonators with magnetic walls, IEEE T-MTT 26(2), 1978

archetypes.name: Annular ring patch
archetypes.summary: Microstrip ring resonating where its mean circumference is a guided wavelength; markedly smaller than a disc at the same frequency.

synthesis.notes: Narrow-ring rule k*r_mean = 1 (mean circumference = one guided wavelength), corrected by a cubic fitted to exact roots of the Bessel cross-product. Worst error 0.20% over b/a from 1.05 to 5, against 2.71% for the uncorrected rule.

analysis.notes: The EXACT TM11 condition J1'(ka)Y1'(kb) - J1'(kb)Y1'(ka), which vanishes at resonance. Non-zero here measures how far the fitted design rule sits from the true root, so it is a live check on the synthesis rather than a restatement of it.
radius a circular patch would need at the same frequency, from the first root of J1'
About 0.74 at b/a = 2: the ring's outer radius is a quarter smaller than a disc's, and its area roughly halved
Indicative placeholder. The TM11 ring radiates broadside much as a disc does, a little lower for the smaller aperture.
Narrow-ring approximation: the TM_n1 modes sit where the circumference is n wavelengths, so TM21 lands near 2*f0. The exact roots drift from this as the ring widens.

validity: 1.05 < b/a < 5, the range the correction was fitted over
cavity model with magnetic side walls and no fringing correction on the radii: real rings resonate a few percent low
the exact resonance is transcendental; resonance_residual reports how far the design rule sits from it
feeding a ring is awkward - a probe, a coupled microstrip line or an aperture all perturb the mode differently

known_cases.source: At b/a = 1.2 the exact root is k*r_mean = 1.0014, and the fitted rule reproduces it closely enough that the exact Bessel cross-product very nearly vanishes. Roots found independently by bisection on the cross-product.
b/a = 2: exact k*r_mean = 1.0160, fitted 1.0151. The residual stays small; the uncorrected narrow-ring rule would leave a 1.6% frequency error here.
Outer radius 1.3534/k against a disc's 1.8412/k: 26% smaller in radius and 46% smaller in area at the same frequency

references: Garg, Bhartia, Bahl & Ittipiboon, Microstrip Antenna Design Handbook, Artech 2001, Ch. 8
Chew, A broad-band annular-ring microstrip antenna, IEEE T-AP 30(5), 1982
Exact roots computed here by bisection on the Bessel cross-product; the design rule is a fit to them

archetypes.name: Truncated-corner circularly polarised patch
archetypes.summary: Square patch with two opposite corners cut away, splitting one feed into two degenerate modes in quadrature.

synthesis.notes: first estimate of the side, used only to evaluate eps_reff - a square patch has W = L, so the usual width formula does not apply
one iteration; a second pass moves it by well under a percent
From dS/S = 1/(2Q), with Q taken from the patch bandwidth as Q = 1/(BW*sqrt(2)), so dS/S = BW/sqrt(2). The two cut triangles have combined area c^2, so c/L = sqrt(dS/S).

analysis.notes: square patch, so W/L = 1
inverted from BW = (S-1)/(Q*sqrt(S)) at S = 2
dS/S, the classic single-feed CP condition. A high-Q patch needs only a tiny cut, which is exactly why single-feed CP is so sensitive to etching tolerance.
The two degenerate modes must be separated by f0/(2Q) for 90 degrees of phase difference at f0
Indicative: the 3 dB axial-ratio band of a single-feed CP patch is typically about a third of its impedance band. A dual-feed patch with a quadrature hybrid is far wider, at the cost of the hybrid.
as a linear square patch; the truncation is too small to change the aperture
by construction at exactly f0, where the mode split gives precisely 90 degrees

validity: the dS/S = 1/(2Q) rule assumes the two modes are otherwise degenerate and equally excited, which requires the feed on a diagonal
single-feed CP is narrowband in axial ratio - a few tenths of a percent on thin high-permittivity substrates
sense of rotation is set by WHICH diagonal is cut; this spec does not track handedness
axial ratio degrades rapidly off boresight and off frequency; only the on-axis, on-frequency value is claimed

known_cases.source: 1.6 mm on eps_r = 2.2 at 2.4 GHz gives BW = 1.197%, so Q = 59.05 and dS/S = 1/(2Q) = 0.847%. The truncation leg is sqrt(dS/S) = 9.2% of the side. Garg et al., Microstrip Antenna Design Handbook, Ch. 10
perfect circular polarisation at the design frequency is the definition of the condition, not a prediction

references: Garg, Bhartia, Bahl & Ittipiboon, Microstrip Antenna Design Handbook, Artech 2001, Ch. 10

archetypes.name: Stacked (parasitically coupled) patch
archetypes.summary: A second patch suspended above the driven one, giving two coupled resonances and several times the bandwidth.

parameters.name: patch separation
parameters.description: gap between patches, in free-space wavelengths

synthesis.notes: The parasitic is deliberately detuned so the two resonances straddle f0. Sitting in a lower-permittivity medium, it is usually made slightly SMALLER than the driven patch for the same resonance.

analysis.notes: the driven patch on its own
The honest cost. Most of the bandwidth comes from the extra height, not from the coupling as such.

INDICATIVE AND NOT DERIVED. Published stacked patches report roughly 2 to 3 times a single patch's bandwidth for a well-chosen gap and size ratio. Treat as a rough expectation, not a design figure; the real answer needs a coupled-resonator solve or a full-wave simulation.
the single-patch expression evaluated at the TOTAL height and multiplied by the indicative coupling factor - compounding two approximations, so treat the result as an order of magnitude
Indicative: a little above a single patch, since the stack is electrically taller. Placeholder.

validity: LOW CONFIDENCE: the bandwidth multiplier is an expectation drawn from published designs, not a computed result
the optimum gap and size ratio interact strongly; both are inputs here and neither is optimised
surface waves grow with total height and are not modelled - they eat efficiency exactly where this design gains bandwidth
a probe feeding through both substrates adds inductance that often dominates the match on thick stacks

known_cases.source: Geometry only, which is the part of this archetype that is actually derived: a 0.03-wavelength gap at 2.4 GHz is 3.75 mm, making the stack 0.043 wavelengths tall in all.
parasitic at 0.95 of the driven patch's 41.32 mm length

references: Waterhouse, Stacked patches for broadband microstrip antennas, Electronics Letters 35(2), 1999
Garg, Bhartia, Bahl & Ittipiboon, Microstrip Antenna Design Handbook, Artech 2001, Ch. 9.3
